recent_posts.title: Matthias Endler
recent_posts.summary: A personal reflection on the nature of taste, distinguishing it from mere preference and expertise. Through examples like Willie Nelson's guitar and blog design evolution, the author argues that good taste requires deep contextual knowledge, obsessive attention to detail, and the wisdom to know what to leave out. Algorithms and mass-market brands are identified as enemies of developing genuine taste, while caring deeply about something — anything — is offered as the path forward.

recent_posts.title: Why personal blogging still matters in the age of AI
recent_posts.summary: Personal blogging remains valuable in an era of AI-generated content because readers crave authentic human perspectives. Just as people still watch human chess players despite machines being superior at the game for decades, audiences prefer reading genuine thoughts from real people over algorithmic content. Writing a personal blog offers both the satisfaction of helping others and the personal benefit of clarifying one's own thinking.

recent_posts.title: Building Up And Sanding Down
recent_posts.summary: Two complementary approaches to building software systems are explored: building up (starting with a solid foundation and gradually adding functionality) and sanding down (starting with a rough prototype and iteratively refining it). Building up works well for known domains with clear specifications, emphasizing correctness and strong abstractions from the start. Sanding down suits creative projects requiring experimentation, focusing on rapid iteration and deferring perfectionism. The choice depends on team dynamics, problem familiarity, and project nature. Examples include implementing protocols with Rust's type system versus iterating on game mechanics with minimal framework overhead.

recent_posts.title: On Choosing Rust
recent_posts.summary: Addresses common criticisms and misconceptions about adopting Rust in established software projects like git and coreutils. Debunks claims about Rust's performance limitations, security benefits, and motivations behind language adoption. Argues that Rust adoption is driven by practical concerns like memory safety and maintainability rather than hype, citing real-world examples and production use cases.

recent_posts.title: How To Review Code
recent_posts.summary: A comprehensive guide to effective code reviewing based on two decades of experience. Emphasizes focusing on big picture design over syntax, the critical importance of good naming, being decisive when rejecting changes, and treating reviews as iterative communication processes. Key principles include running code locally when possible, asking clarifying questions, avoiding nitpicking on formatting, and continuously learning from the review process.

recent_posts.title: Why copying code can be better than premature abstraction
recent_posts.summary: The DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principle is often misapplied in software development. Copying code can actually be beneficial for maintaining momentum, discovering the right abstractions naturally, and avoiding premature optimization. Wrong abstractions are harder to remove than duplicated code and create mental overhead through multiple layers of indirection. The key is separating writing mode from refactoring mode, allowing duplication initially, and cleaning up once you understand the problem better. Sometimes similar-looking code serves different purposes and should remain separate to preserve context and enable independent evolution.

recent_posts.title: Stop watching millionaires and start living your own life
recent_posts.summary: A personal reflection on how modern media consumption revolves around watching wealthy celebrities and public figures, from sports stars to actors to musicians. The author observes how normalized it has become to focus on millionaires and billionaires while overlooking ordinary people and their stories. The piece encourages readers to seek out smaller voices, share their own experiences, and live authentically rather than constantly consuming other people's lives.

recent_posts.title: Paolo the Plumber
recent_posts.summary: A parable about Paolo, a skilled plumber who faces competition from his friend Mario's automated plumbing machine. While the machine initially appears faster and cheaper, it produces poor quality work with improperly sealed pipes and unnecessary additions. Paolo's traditional craftsmanship becomes valuable again as customers return to fix the machine's mistakes. The story illustrates the tension between automation and skilled craftsmanship, highlighting how over-reliance on tools without understanding fundamentals can lead to quality issues and dependency.

recent_posts.title: Why reinventing the wheel fuels innovation
recent_posts.summary: Reinventing the wheel is often discouraged, yet it plays a crucial role in learning and innovation. By creating toy versions of known concepts, individuals deepen their understanding and explore new possibilities. The process can reveal complexities in seemingly simple ideas and allows for creative problem-solving. Balancing the reuse of established solutions with personal experimentation fosters both insight and impact.

recent_posts.title: No Matter What
recent_posts.summary: Establishing strict 'no matter what' rules, like having dinner at 6pm every day, creates consistency and positively impacts daily life. These rules may seem simple but require dedication and can lead to deeper relationships and more structured lives. Starting with small responsibilities, such as caring for plants, can help in forming these habits.
